en: The Sūtra on Loving Oneself, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...

The king went to where the Buddha was; seeing the vihāra from afar, he descended from his carriage and set aside his parasol. He unsheathed his sword, removed his shoes, and advanced directly with hands clasped in reverence. Prostrating himself on the ground, he bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to kneel upright and said:
“I pray that you and the Sangha will accept my invitation for tomorrow at the crossroads of the four main streets, where I shall provide a modest meal.”
May he cause all ignorant folk to know that the Buddha is most supreme, so that upon beholding his rites, they may transmit them as a model for generations.
May he cause sentient beings to distance themselves from ghosts, demons, and sorcery, and to fully observe the five precepts, thereby extinguishing the calamities of the state!
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent!
As a king, one ought to provide wise guidance, leading the people by means of the Way and seeking future blessings."

In the past, when I was a king, I also made offerings to the Buddhas, śramaṇas, and brahmins; I constantly practiced the four immeasurables and the six perfections, striving diligently to attain Buddhahood, which is majestic and unsurpassed.
The king said:
“O Most Truthful One!
It is indeed as the Buddha has taught: for one who does not plant a seed, there is no way to obtain its fruit.”

I have received the Buddha’s grace by being born into this world as a human; having left the female state to become male, my six sense-faculties are fully intact. Amidst such a convergence of great blessings, I have encountered the Buddha dwelling in the world, and the flourishing and brilliant transformation of the Dharma has reached my country—my accumulation of merit is immeasurable.
"I request to retire; please prepare everything with solemnity.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent, excellent!"
The king immediately returned to the palace and leveled the great road, making it smooth and even throughout its rises and falls;
he extensively set up canopies and curtains, and erected various banners and streamers.
From the crossroads to the gate of the vihāra, railings were placed along both sides of the road, with lamps arrayed like stars and incense burners at every step.
The celestial musicians performed various arts, singing of the spiritual majesty of the Buddha, the Most Honored One, and extolling the pure and chaste virtue of the śramaṇa;
they scattered flowers and miscellaneous jewels that fell profusely like rain, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, and spread out fine carpets.
The King personally prepared a meal throughout the night and went in person to welcome [the Buddha], prostrating himself on the ground and kneeling for a long time, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will bestow great compassion and manifest his form to save all sentient beings!"
The Buddha rose, donned his dharma robes, and went with the śramaṇas to the crossroads.
The king and his ministers escorted him on the left and right; when the Buddha arrived, he took his seat.
The lady and the crown prince both prostrated themselves upon the ground, baring their arms and washing their feet barefoot.
Having offered the water for rinsing, they personally served the food with their own hands.
When the Buddha had finished his meal, they prostrated themselves and said:

"I now provide this modest meal; I pray that gods, humans, ghosts, dragons, winged creatures, crawling insects, and all wriggling life-forms may, in every successive birth, encounter the Buddha, encounter the Dharma, and encounter the community of śramaṇas, thereby casting off worldly filth and stench and cherishing the Buddha’s true and correct teaching."
The Buddha said, “Excellent!
As a father and mother to the people, you have moistened them with compassion and guided them with great wisdom; what you wish for shall surely be attained!”
The King said:
"When the people throughout the land part from one another, they all say, 'Take care of yourself.
Is there a fundamental meaning to this expression 'take care of yourself'?"
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent is your question!

When a person dwells in the world, harboring poisonous thoughts in the mind, uttering poisonous words with the mouth, and performing poisonous deeds with the body—these three matters arising from the mind, body, and mouth proclaim their own evil and inflict it upon sentient beings."
When sentient beings are afflicted by poison, they immediately harbor resentment and vow in their hearts to take revenge, whether seeking retribution in the present life or,
after the body has perished, having their souls ascend to heaven to descend and settle the score.
Among humans, animals, ghosts, spirits, and those in the Mount Tai hells, they harm and prey upon one another; all this arises from past karma and does not occur by chance.
If one commits no evil through the three acts of the body, the four of the mouth, or the three of the mind, yet the fool indulges in them and is unfilial toward his parents;

if he reveres ghosts and demons, engages in licentiousness, and is reckless with wine, thereby descending into the turbidity of the base and lowly, he will bring about the calamity of endangering himself and exterminating his clan. After death, he enters the Mount Tai hells of boiling water and fire, where he shall long fail to obtain a human body. Straying far from the Buddha and the Right Way, he takes no pleasure in the pure precepts of the śramaṇa and constantly associates with fools.
"This means that one who delights in the calamity of ruin and destruction is one who does not love themselves!
The King said, "Excellent, excellent! Only the Buddha’s instruction and admonition are thus!"
"I wish to hear the principles for loving oneself;
what are they? The Buddha said:

"The method for loving oneself is to first take the three refuges, to nourish one's kin through the Dharma, to love all beings with compassion, to feel pity for those who are ignorant and deluded, to rejoice in seeing the right path and to advance therein, to protect all equally and universally, to bring peace and relief to sentient beings, to bestow these four debts of gratitude, and to give alms to the poor and destitute."

Sentient beings will be free from enmity; the devas will protect and nurture them; no calamities shall befall them; imprisonment, sharp swords, and all poisons shall be extinguished; their kin will be at peace and their clans will flourish; they will be free from misfortune and affliction during life, and upon death, they will ascend to heaven and constantly encounter the light.
"This is what is called loving oneself!
The King said, "Excellent!"
"Only the Buddha’s admonitions!
Truly, you are a man of noble conduct and virtue, pure and chaste, guarding the truth;
you are not defiled in heart by sordid gain or perverse pleasures."
Maintain silence with the four gates of speech; let the three types of misfortune remain far from your person.
To preserve one's life while perfecting one's conduct is what all Buddhas treasure;
when parents are at peace and the clan prospers, one shall ultimately ascend to heaven.
"One who constantly attains assemblies of merit is what is called a person who loves themselves. The King said:
"Excellent! Only the Buddha's teaching is true!
"Though various poisons were heaped upon me, I endured them in silence and did not speak;"
With compassion and pity for others, one should provide them with relief from beginning to end;
with diligent effort and without indolence, one should uphold the Three Honored Ones in mind;
remaining outwardly tranquil and inwardly serene, one should cultivate mindfulness as the root of the Path.
Profoundly contemplating the noble path, he clearly elucidated the transformation of mantras;
filial toward his parents and self-reliant, he led the multitude to follow suit,
constantly meeting with blessings.
"This is what is called loving oneself!
The King said, "Excellent!"
"Only the Buddha’s teaching is true!
Countless people observed this, at which time there were two merchants, one of whom thought to himself:
"The Buddha's body is sixteen feet tall, with a golden-purple hue; his head is crowned with a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), and his neck radiates the light of the sun—his majesty is beyond words."
The Buddha is like an emperor, and the śramaṇas are like loyal ministers.
The Buddha proclaims the luminous Dharma, and the śramaṇas recite and propagate it.
This king is enlightened; he knows that the Buddha is worthy of veneration!
The Buddha, knowing his thought, gazed intently at him; the man’s heart was filled with joy, as if he had found a treasure.
Another man thought to himself:
“This king is foolish and deluded; you are the sovereign of the nation, so what more could you possibly seek?”
The Buddha is like an ox, and his disciples are like a cart.
Just as that ox pulls the cart to the east, west, south,
or north, so it is with the Buddha.
"What path do you possess that you have humbled yourself to serve it?
The Buddha, knowing that he harbored evil thoughts and would surely incur calamity, felt deep compassion for him.
The man was struck with fear, as if he had encountered something ominous.
The two men departed together and stayed overnight at a distance of thirty li. They purchased wine and drank it while discussing their respective affairs; their disputes were numerous and confused.
As for those who possessed virtuous thoughts, the Four Heavenly Kings dispatched benevolent deities to protect them.

As for those who slander the Buddha with a poisonous mind, the ghosts of Mount Tai cause wine to enter their intestines as if fire were burning their bodies; they emerge and lie prostrate by the roadside, immediately tumbling into the ruts of a carriage track.
At dawn, a merchant’s caravan of five hundred chariots ran over and killed him. His companions sought him out and saw him;
he said, "I am ruined!

Upon returning to his kingdom, he was suspected of having taken goods and fled, which he considered unrighteous. He thus abandoned his body and his wealth and departed. Wandering far away, he traveled tens of thousands of li from Śrāvastī.
There was a kingdom where the king had passed away and there was no crown prince. A prophetic book stated:
"In the central land there is a humble man who shall reign over this territory.
The assembled officials deliberated, saying:
"A state without a ruler is like a body without a head; it is difficult for such a state to endure!
Therefore, when there is a horse, it always performs the ritual of submission to the King.
If there were one who could fulfill the role of King, the horse would surely kneel before him!"
They all replied, "Excellent!

They immediately prepared a grand carriage, placed the royal seal and ribbon upon it, and set out with men and horses filling the roads; among those who watched, there were none who did not shed tears.
The merchant also went out to observe, and the Grand Historian of the state said:
"That canopy of yellow clouds—this is a divine omen!
The divine horse galloped straight forward, knelt down, and licked the merchant’s feet.
The ministers were filled with joy; they bathed him in fragrant water and prostrated themselves, installing him as king, and all unanimously declared themselves his subjects.
The king said:
"I was originally a merchant and have no merit toward the people; I am unfit for this celestial station!"
The officials said,
“Devadatta possesses virtue, for the divine horse has knelt before him! Thereupon,
he took up residence in the royal palace and oversaw the administration of state affairs.
He reflected deeply, saying:
"I possess no subtle merit; by what cause have I obtained this?
It must surely be the Buddha’s grace that has brought it about!"
At dawn, while seated upon his throne, he marveled at the unsurpassed holiness of the Buddha; leading his ministers, he bowed his head toward Śrāvastī and said:
"A lowly man, having received the moistening grace of the World-Honored One, has attained the status of a human king."
Throughout the generations of this land, it has been transmitted that there was no knowledge of the Buddha;
even among the secular books of common custom, there is no record of him.
I pray that through this great illumination, you will open the eyes of the deaf and blind among the people of this nation!
"I pray that tomorrow you and the assembly of Arhats will deign to turn your attention toward this single occasion for three months!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Command all the bhikṣus!"
"Tomorrow that king shall invite us; we shall all gradually manifest transformations and display our sublime spiritual virtues, so that the people of his kingdom may all behold them together!

When the various devas heard that the Buddha had arrived there to teach and transform, they led one another in procession as attendants, performing music and singing praises of his virtue. Precious canopies, banners, and streamers were arrayed, and flowers fell in profusion, their brilliant colors dazzling the eyes of men.

The Buddha and the Arhats were all seated in the main hall. Following the example of the King of Śrāvastī’s offering of the Bright Dharma, the king personally served the food until it was finished; he then sat before the Buddha on a small stool, and the Buddha extensively expounded the Dharma.
The king said, "I am but a man of humble station and have never possessed superior virtue; by what cause have I obtained this?
The Buddha told the king:
"Formerly, when that king provided a meal for the Buddha, he thought to himself:
'The Buddha is like a king, and the śramaṇas are like his subjects.
Having planted this seed, the king now reaps its fruit."
One person said:
"If the Buddha were an ox, his disciples would be like a cart.
He himself planted the seeds that were crushed by the wheels of a cart; now he is being crushed by the wheels of a fire-cart in Mount Tai, having reaped the fruit of his own actions.
This is not something that can be brought about by a king’s valor or prowess!

When one does good, blessings follow; when one practices evil, calamity pursues. As an echo responds to a sound, so do good and evil correspond to their causes. It is not wrought by devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits, nor is it wrought by ancestral spirits; it is the mind that creates it, which then manifests through body and speech.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
If one commits evil within the mind, and immediately speaks or acts upon it, suffering follows as surely as a wheel follows the track of its ruts."
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign and the mind is the driver.
When one conceives of goodness within the mind, it immediately issues in speech and action; thus, merit and happiness follow of their own accord, like a shadow following a form.
The World-Honored One further addressed the king, saying:
"Among the sins of all evils, there are five that are most grave.
To be unfilial and disloyal, to kill one's parents or sovereign, and thereby cause the destruction of a family or the chaos of a state—this is the first heavy crime."

The practice of the Arhats involves attaining the concentrations of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness; they align their intentions with those of the Buddha to rescue and deliver sentient beings. To be ignorant toward them constitutes the second grave offense.

The Buddha is one whose manifold transgressions have been exhausted and whose great blessings have fully matured; endowed with the marks and signs and the ten powers, he guides sentient beings through the Dharma. His compassion, kindness, and protective care exceed that of a loving mother, yet to foolishly slander him is the third grave offense.
The pure śramaṇas possess lofty aspirations and noble conduct;
cherishing the sūtras and the Dharma, they assist the Buddha in transforming the ignorant.
That the Buddhas succeed one another and that sentient beings attain liberation all depend upon the Saṃgha.
When flatterers and slanderers conspire together, it leads to disharmony.
When the Sangha is disharmonious, the righteous Dharma is destroyed and the people run wild.
That the righteous Dharma is destroyed and the people run wild causes the three paths to flourish and afflicts the Bhikṣu-saṅgha; this is the fourth grave offense.

The Buddha’s sacred shrines, their precious objects, water, and soil are offered with sincere hearts by sentient beings to the Triple Gem; if a fool should destroy or steal them, it is the fifth grave offense.
To commit any of these five offenses is to incur a crime for which there is no pardon; it is called taking one's own life, destroying one's own clan, and casting oneself into the fires of Mount Tai.
The gravity of these five crimes exceeds that of Mount Sumeru; be careful not to transgress them!

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the king and his ministers all attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) and received the five precepts to become lay devotees (*upāsaka*).

Among the citizens, some became śramaṇas while others observed the precepts as lay devotees; they subsequently established the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths as the state policy. Protected by the various devas, the kingdom then flourished.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and common people were all filled with joy.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Ātmavatsa-sūtra*.
